newsitem.title: USA: Dlr recovers from overnight lows to end up in U.S.
newsitem.headline: Dlr recovers from overnight lows to end up in U.S.

text.p: The dollar recovered in U.S. trade to close higher against the yen and mark after a push lower overseas met its downside targets and then lost momentum, traders said.
The dollar was forced below critical support levels at 1.5050 marks and 110.80 yen in technically-driven trade overseas before a significant number of buyers were enticed.

"The sell-off bottomed right at the New York opening as we saw some very good buying interest under 110.70 yen and 1.5050 marks," said Ben Strauss, associate vice-president at Bank Julius Baer and Co.
The dollar closed higher at 1.5090/95 marks compared to 1.5040/50 marks at Friday's open. Against the yen, the dollar finished at 111.05/10, up from 110.55/65 at the open.
Many traders were caught ill positioned, having bought yen and sold Swiss francs and marks, when the dollar/yen market began to move higher.
Dealers scrambled to sell yen to cover outstanding positions, which aided the dollar, dealers said.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's affirmation in late-trade Thursday of his longstanding strong-dollar policy also helped to stop the dollar's slide overseas, dealers said.

"Without a change in Rubin's strong-dollar stance, it's hard to warrant really pushing the move a lot lower, especially with the 110 dollar/yen psychological level being so close," said Seth Garrett, chief dealer at CS First Boston.
The dollar gained after hitting a fresh 49-month low against the British pound of $1.6680 in overseas trade to higher at $1.6628/38 from Friday's open of $1.6660/70.
Dealers sold pounds for dollars to lock in profits earned from the pound's recent meteoric rise against both the dollar and mark.

Strong recent British economic data which suggest higher interest rates in the near future have fueled the sharp gains in sterling. Rising British rates would increase returns on investments in pound-denominated assets.

Dealers sold Swiss francs, mostly against the yen, after the Swiss government said its pension funds, with invested assets estimated at close to 30 billion Swiss francs, may now place some of their holdings in bonds in foreign currencies.
"There is some concern over increased capital outflows out of Switzerland, which is more bearish news for the Swiss franc," Strauss said.
"To add to the flames, mark/Swiss has been moving steadily higher for several weeks and that has increased the pressure on the Swiss franc."
The dollar closed higher at 1.2783/93 Swiss francs from 1.2745/55 at Friday's open.
In other trading, the dollar ended at Canadian $1.3388/93, down from C$1.3390/95 at the open.
The Australian dollar ended $0.7901/06, up from $0.7905/10.
